h1:
Wang Takrai, Nakhon Nayok
A Shady Stream Park for Shallow Swimming and Family Camping
intro: Wang Takrai is a private forest park of more than 1,500 rai along a stream in Mueang Nakhon Nayok district. The draw is the clear, shallow water running over the rocks, with shade all day long, so kids can splash around easily. There are camping grounds and riverside cabins too, making it a spot Bangkok families drive out to for a day trip or an overnight stay.

blocks.html: If you want to escape the heat without a long drive, Wang Takrai is the answer Bangkok folks have turned to for years. It sits in Sarika sub-district, Mueang Nakhon Nayok, just over two hours' drive from Bangkok. This isn't a thundering waterfall crashing down a cliff — it's a clear stream drifting gently over rocks beneath big shade trees, shallow enough for kids to wade in all day. That's exactly why so many families pick this place over the more powerful falls.

Wang Takrai is a private forest park, developed by M.C. Bhisadej Rajani decades ago, so ornamental flowers and plants are scattered across the whole area. The vibe lands somewhere between a botanical garden and a swimming spot. The water comes from Mae Plong Waterfall and Heo Krathin Waterfall, two streams that meet inside the park, which is why there's water to play in almost all year round.

blocks.text: What swimming at Wang Takrai is like

blocks.html: The heart of Wang Takrai is the shallow stream that stretches across several stretches. The water is clear enough to see the sandy bottom, only knee- to waist-deep in the main swimming spots, so small kids can wade in with an adult close by, while the grown-ups sit and soak their feet on the cool rocks all day. A few stretches run a little deeper for anyone who wants to drift along on a tube.

items: Tube rental — available all along the stream, around 40 THB per tube, in several sizes for both kids and adults.
Mat / seating rental — mats laid out by the water rent for about 30 THB, holding your spot for the whole day.
Showers and toilets — spread across several points in the park, so you can rinse off and change after swimming.
Riverside food stalls — there are made-to-order food stalls and drinks on site; order and eat right by the stream.

blocks.title: Water levels by season
blocks.html: Late rainy season into early winter (October–December) brings the most water and the clearest conditions, so it's the most fun. During the dry months around March–April the water drops, and some spots leave only enough for soaking your feet. If you're set on a proper swim, skip the dry season.

blocks.html: You can stay overnight at Wang Takrai either in a tent or a cabin. The camping ground sits right by the stream, so you wake up and walk just a few steps down to the water. It suits families who want their kids to sleep out in nature without it being too rough, since the toilets and food stalls are close by. If you'd rather not haul gear, there are cabins in several sizes to choose from, from small ones for couples to larger ones that sleep the whole family.

items.name: Streamside camping ground
items.blurb: Flat ground under the shade trees right by the water. Bring your own tent, wake up and walk straight down for a swim. Great for budget-minded campers.

items.name: Mid-size to large cabins
items.blurb: Several cabins scattered through the park, some right by the water, sleeping anywhere from 2 people to the whole family. Book ahead on long weekends.

blocks.title: Book your stay ahead
blocks.html: Long weekends and the cool season get very busy, and the good cabins and camping spots fill up fast. Call ahead to book at 081 989 0365 or 037 385 164. Checking availability before you drive out gives you peace of mind.

blocks.text: Beyond swimming, what else is there to do

blocks.html: Because it started life as a plant garden, Wang Takrai has more places to stroll than your average waterfall. You can wander among the ornamental flowers, take photos under the big trees, or bike around the grounds. There's a mini zoo for the kids to see animals, and a café to sit and sip coffee. The whole place stays shady and cool even when the sun is blazing.

items: Stroll the flower garden — ornamental flowers and plants are planted throughout, with naturally pretty photo spots.
Mini zoo — lets the kids see animals up close during a break from swimming.
Café in the garden — sit and sip coffee among the trees, a good rest stop for adults who'd rather not get in the water.
Streamside picnic — bring a mat and some food and settle in under the shade trees for the whole day.

blocks.text: Entry fees, opening hours and getting there

blocks.html: The entry fee is charged per vehicle, not per head like the state-run waterfalls. It's about 150 THB per car (up to 8 passengers; beyond that there's an extra 10 THB per person). It's open daily, roughly 08:00–18:00. Getting there is easy: if you drive yourself from Bangkok, take the Rangsit–Ongkharak–Nakhon Nayok route, then turn off toward Sarika. The signs are clear and a regular sedan can reach it without trouble.

items: Entry fee — about 150 THB per car (up to 8 people); over that, an extra 10 THB per person.
From Bangkok — drive ~2 hrs via Ongkharak into Mueang Nakhon Nayok, then on toward Sarika.
Car rental / taxi — without your own car, you can arrange a charter ride from Nakhon Nayok town, since little public transport reaches the spot directly.

blocks.title: Weekdays have the edge
blocks.html: Saturdays, Sundays and long weekends get crowded, and the main swimming stretch of the stream fills up. If you can choose, go on a weekday for quieter corners, clearer water and far easier parking.
If you want to make the overnight worth it, here's an easy plan where the kids have fun and the adults don't wear out — swimming in the morning and evening, plenty of rest in between.

items.note: Drive through Ongkharak, stop to grab some snacks for the car, reach Nakhon Nayok mid-morning.

blocks.text: The honest truth before you go

blocks.html: Straight up: Wang Takrai isn't the place for anyone after a big, dramatic waterfall. It's a shallow stream that stands out for its shade and suits kids more than thrills. If you love jumping into deep water or powerful falls, Sarika or Nang Rong Waterfall will suit you better.

items: Charged per car — the more of you there are, the better the value; going solo feels a bit pricey.
Genuinely crowded on holidays — festival periods are packed and noisy; for quiet, go on a weekday.
Low water in the dry season — in March–April some spots leave only enough for soaking your feet, so check water conditions before you go.
Food inside the park costs more than outside — on a tight budget, you can bring your own water and snacks.

faq.q: How much is the entry fee at Wang Takrai?
faq.a: It's charged per vehicle, about 150 THB per car for up to 8 passengers; beyond that it's an extra 10 THB per person. It isn't charged per head like the state-run waterfalls, so it works out better value when you come as a group.

faq.q: Can you swim at Wang Takrai, and is it okay for kids?
faq.a: Yes, you can swim, and it's great for kids — it's a shallow, clear stream drifting gently along, only knee- to waist-deep at the main spots. There are tubes to rent for about 40 THB, but an adult should always stay close.

faq.q: Can you camp at Wang Takrai?
faq.a: Yes. There's a camping ground right by the stream where you can bring your own tent, close to the toilets and food stalls. If you'd rather not haul gear, there are cabins in several sizes. On long weekends, call ahead to book.

faq.q: What time does Wang Takrai open?
faq.a: It's open daily, from roughly 08:00 to 18:00. Mornings are best for clearer water and fewer people than the afternoon, especially on holidays.

faq.q: When is the water highest at Wang Takrai?
faq.a: The water is highest and clearest in late rainy season into early winter, around October to December. During the dry months of March–April the water drops, with some spots leaving only enough to soak your feet.
